client: Losing my job last month has really thrown me off. I’ve been feeling so overwhelmed thinking about money and how I’m going to make ends meet. Plus, every time I try to update my resume, I freeze up—I don’t even know where to start or how to make myself stand out. I guess I’m skeptical therapy can really help with something so practical, but I’m here because I don’t know what else to do.
therapist: It sounds like this situation has left you feeling stuck and uncertain, especially with the practical pressures weighing on you. When you think about updating your resume, what’s the specific thought or worry that makes you freeze up?

client: I keep thinking that no matter what I put on my resume, it won't be good enough. Like, who would want to hire someone who got laid off? I stare at the blank document and just feel worthless, like all my past experience doesn't count for anything now. It's stupid because logically I know people get laid off all the time, but it still feels personal.
therapist: It sounds like you’re caught between recognizing logically that layoffs happen and feeling personally defeated by it—that’s such a hard place to be. When you say you feel worthless, do you notice any specific memories or thoughts that seem to reinforce that feeling?

client: I think part of it is that my last boss made some comments about how I wasn’t “adapting fast enough” to changes in the company. I keep replaying that in my head, and it makes me feel like I’m just not good enough for any job. I know I shouldn’t let one person’s opinion define me, but it’s hard not to when it feels like they were right—I did lose my job, after all.
therapist: It sounds like that comment from your boss has really stuck with you, even though logically you know one person’s opinion doesn’t define your worth. What would it feel like to challenge that thought—to look for evidence that you *are* adaptable and capable, even if this one situation didn’t go as planned?

client: I can think of times when I did adapt well at work—like when I learned that new software system last year. But part of me wants to argue that those successes don't count anymore because I still ended up unemployed. It's like my brain dismisses anything good when I'm feeling like this. And honestly, trying to list my strengths just makes me more anxious because what if I'm wrong about them?
therapist: It sounds like your mind is quick to dismiss the positive examples, even though you can recall them—almost as if it’s protecting itself from disappointment. When you think about listing your strengths, what’s the specific fear that comes up about being wrong?

client: I think the fear is that if I list my strengths and then still don’t get hired, it’ll prove I’m not actually as good as I thought I was. It’s like setting myself up for failure. And I know that’s probably irrational, but it feels safer to just avoid it altogether. Maybe I’m just scared of trying and still ending up in the same place.
therapist: It sounds like you’re caught in a cycle of fearing failure so much that it feels safer not to try at all—but avoiding it keeps you stuck, which only reinforces those fears. What would it feel like to take one small step—like jotting down just one strength—without worrying about the outcome?

client: I guess I could try writing down one strength, but it feels kind of pointless if I don’t believe it’ll actually help me get a job. And I’m worried that once I start, I’ll just start criticizing myself and end up feeling worse. It’s like, why bother if it’s just going to make me feel more inadequate?
therapist: It sounds like you’re anticipating that even trying will lead to self-criticism, which makes it feel like there’s no point in starting. What would it feel like to approach this as an experiment—just noting one strength without judging its impact right away, and seeing what happens?

client: An experiment sounds less intimidating, I guess. I could try writing down one strength, like being organized—I’ve always been good at keeping track of details. But I still feel like it won’t really change anything—it’s just a piece of paper. And I’m worried I’ll start thinking about all the ways I’m *not* organized and spiral from there. It’s hard to believe one small thing could make a difference.
therapist: It sounds like you’re willing to try, but there’s still a lot of doubt and fear lingering—like this one small step might not be enough to shift things. What would it feel like to focus on the act of writing it down itself, rather than worrying about whether it’ll change everything right away?

client: Focusing just on writing it down feels a little less overwhelming—I guess I don’t have to solve everything right now. But I still worry that it’s just avoiding the bigger problem of actually finding a job. It’s like, okay, I can write down that I’m organized, but what does that really do? It doesn’t pay the bills or get me interviews. It feels like I’m wasting time when I should be doing something more practical.
therapist: It sounds like you're balancing between wanting to take a small step and feeling pressured to solve the bigger problem immediately—that tension makes sense when the stakes feel so high. What if we treated this as building a foundation, where acknowledging your strengths isn’t about avoiding the practical steps, but preparing you to approach them with more confidence? How does that idea sit with you?

client: I guess I can see how acknowledging my strengths might help me feel more confident, but it still feels like such a small piece of the puzzle. I’m worried that even if I do this, I’ll still feel stuck when it comes to the bigger tasks like applying for jobs or networking. It’s hard to believe that focusing on my strengths will actually make a difference in the end.
therapist: It sounds like you can see some potential in this approach, but there’s still a lot of doubt about whether it will really help with the bigger challenges ahead—that’s understandable when so much feels at stake. What would it feel like to take this one step at a time, focusing on building confidence first, and then seeing how it might help you approach those bigger tasks?

client: I can try the one-step-at-a-time approach, but it's frustrating because bills are due now, you know? Part of me feels like I don't have the luxury to work on confidence when I need to be sending out applications yesterday. But I also see how panicking and sending out half-hearted applications might not help either. It's just hard to balance.
therapist: It sounds like you're torn between the urgency of practical needs and the worry that rushing might backfire—that's such a difficult tension to hold. What would it look like to carve out even 10 minutes for confidence-building before tackling an application, so it feels less like "either/or"?
